For the Windows 11 transparency requirement, **CaptureGraphicsWin2D is the closest documented fit I found**. ZunShot offers another explicit solution with a straightforward window-selection interface. For the Fedora KDE side, Spectacle has the relevant native window capture controls, although the evidence I inspected does not establish identical corner-alpha behavior on the exact Fedora 45 setup. I could not verify one application that meets the exact requirement on both systems.

### 1. CaptureGraphicsWin2D — Windows window capture with an alpha channel

[CaptureGraphicsWin2D](https://github.com/rednoah/CaptureGraphicsWin2D) describes itself as a Windows 11 screenshot tool that captures windows through Microsoft.Graphics.Win2D and writes PNG files with alpha. Its documentation explicitly covers rounded window borders, window shadows, and transparent surfaces such as the taskbar. That directly addresses the problem of retaining desktop pixels around a rounded window.

The project also documents command-line capture, including targeting a particular window class, so it is relevant if a CLI is acceptable. This is a Windows-specific option; the inspected documentation does not establish Linux, Android, macOS, or Qt 6 support. Its live README has no publication date that I could use to establish availability by 17 November 2026.

### 2. ZunShot — explicit transparent rounded-corner capture

[ZunShot's window-capture guide](https://www.bandicam.com/zunshot/guide/capture-window/) specifically describes making Windows 11 window corners transparent. Choose Window, point at the window, and click; the documented shortcut is Shift+PrtScn. A menu also lets you select an open window by name. Save to PNG or WebP to retain transparency.

The guide says this option is enabled by default and allows its corner radius to be changed. This is useful for the exact visual problem, but it should not be interpreted as proof that arbitrary translucent window materials are reconstructed: the documented feature is rounded-corner transparency. Only the visible portion of a partly off-screen window is captured. If another application pastes white corners, the guide recommends inserting a saved PNG because the receiving application may have selected a clipboard bitmap without alpha. The page is undated, so its availability at the question's cutoff remains unknown.

### 3. KDE Spectacle — the native KDE window-capture route

The [Spectacle handbook](https://docs.kde.org/stable_kf6/en/spectacle/spectacle/spectacle.pdf) documents Active Window and Window Under Cursor capture, PNG saving, and controls for including window decorations. A [dated KDE source-change announcement from 22 October 2023](https://mail.kde.org/pipermail/kde-doc-english/2023-October/024138.html) additionally documents optional window shadows and the corresponding KWin capture options.

For KDE, use one of those window modes and decide whether you need the titlebar, borders, and shadow. This is a useful native candidate, but the inspected evidence does not prove the exact alpha result for every Wayland decoration theme or the stated Fedora release. The dated source establishes the older window/shadow mechanism; the current handbook is live documentation. It does not solve the Windows half of the preference.

### 4. Microsoft's winapp CLI — a scriptable Windows surface-capture option

The [winapp CLI screenshot documentation](https://github.com/microsoft/winappCli/blob/main/docs/ui-automation.md) says its default Windows.Graphics.Capture path preserves rounded corners and transparency and can capture a window even when another window covers it. It can target a window handle and save PNG.

There is a material complication: a window and its owned dialogs can be combined into labeled panels, so an HWND alone does not guarantee a single bare-window image. Element selection changes that behavior. The screen-capture override reads the displayed screen region, and fallback capture modes do not carry the same transparency guarantee. This is an advanced Windows option whose current implementation date is unverified.

I also checked ksnip's primary README. It is a plausible cross-platform editor with window-capture modes, but its platform matrix differs across backends and does not establish transparent DWM corners, so I would not present it as a verified answer to the central requirement. ShareX's indexed issue raised the rounded-corner problem, but the fetched issue extract did not establish a fix.

These findings come from public documentation and source material; I did not install or execute the screenshot tools.

For this prototype, I would put a small parseOptions(String line) adapter around an existing Java option parser. Raw command-line text needs two operations: turn quoted text into argument tokens, then interpret option names and values. The parsers below address the second operation; Ant supplies a useful component for the first. None of the verified parsers alone was established to satisfy the entire raw-string-to-Map requirement.

1. JArgs — best match for a compact, permissively licensed starting point.
https://jargs.sourceforge.net/
Its CmdLineParser supports short and long options, long values with an equals sign, a double-dash terminator, and concatenated boolean short flags. The project describes itself as compact and BSD licensed. Its site dates release 1.0 to 12 April 2005, so this is supported by evidence before the 2 December 2015 cutoff.
https://jargs.sourceforge.net/doc/api/jargs/gnu/CmdLineParser.html
The important limitations are that parse takes String[], returns void, and exposes results through option accessors; your adapter must tokenize the input and construct the desired Map. Its documented concatenated-option behavior rejects a cluster containing an option that requires a value, so do not assume every GNU clustering edge case works. I did not verify the ideal of copying exactly one source file.

2. Apache Commons CLI, particularly the documented 1.3.1 DefaultParser — a practical option-parsing component with dated evidence.
https://commons.apache.org/proper/commons-cli/javadocs/api-release/org/apache/commons/cli/DefaultParser.html
The historical API documents short-option bursting and parsing String[] into CommandLine, with a source revision dated 3 May 2015. Public source also shows handling of long options and an end-of-options prefix.
https://github.com/apache/commons-cli/blob/master/src/main/java/org/apache/commons/cli/DefaultParser.java
Use it after tokenization and copy the resulting options into your own map. It is a library with its own result classes, not a verified single-file implementation. The current source is useful corroboration, but current implementation details are not automatically evidence of 2015 behavior.

3. JOpt Simple — especially useful when a map-shaped result matters.
https://jopt-simple.github.io/jopt-simple/apidocs/joptsimple/OptionParser.html
Its API explicitly documents -abc clustering, long options with equals-sign values, and -- termination. OptionSet.asMap() provides a standard Map, although its keys are OptionSpec objects and its values are lists, so a Map keyed by your own option names still requires conversion.
https://jopt-simple.github.io/jopt-simple/apidocs/joptsimple/OptionSet.html
It also needs already tokenized arguments. The project change log records the map method in version 4.6 and a switch to the MIT license.
https://jopt-simple.github.io/jopt-simple/changes.html
The documentation site is dated 27 November 2018. I am therefore retaining this as later evidence, rather than asserting that the exact inspected version and behavior were available by the cutoff; the date-focused search did not establish a dated older release.

4. Apache Ant Commandline.translateCommandline — a complementary raw-string tokenizer.
https://ant.apache.org/manual/api/org/apache/tools/ant/types/Commandline.html
This static method accepts a String and returns String[]. Its public Java source uses separate ordinary, single-quoted, and double-quoted states, preserves spaces inside quoted arguments, and rejects unbalanced quotes.
https://github.com/apache/ant/blob/master/src/main/org/apache/tools/ant/types/Commandline.java
It can supply the input tokens for one of the option parsers above. It is not itself an option parser, and its small quoting grammar should not be presented as a complete Unix shell lexer: the inspected delimiter set contains ordinary spaces and quotes, and does not establish shell escape, tab-separation, expansion, or substitution semantics. The file carries Apache License 2.0. This live source has no verified pre-cutoff version in this run, so its historical availability is unknown.

For the requested example, the adapter should preserve the message as one token before applying the configured option definitions. Keep non-option operands separately, and consider Map<String, List<String>> if repeated options matter. Both choices make it easier to replace the parser later. This is a proposed integration approach, not a tested implementation.

The public GitHub code-search endpoint was blocked. I used code-through-web search and opened public source pages instead; I am not claiming native code-search success. Apache Commons Exec's string-parsing source was also inspected, but its command/executable model and argument re-quoting make it less direct for this adapter. No claim is made that any candidate was deployed or demonstrated useful in this shell.

# Moving personal email off Google

I would start with a trial of **Purelymail** if the priority is the smallest annual bill, and compare **Migadu Micro** if your mail volume is light. **mailbox Standard** is the next option to examine for more storage at a moderate annual price. **Fastmail Individual** costs more, but its documented JMAP API is a useful bonus if you later connect an AI agent.

These are a shortlist for validation, not a claim that a feature page proves inbox delivery. Your summary provides no maximum budget, delivery-success threshold, mailbox size or export schedule. Those gaps remain explicit rather than becoming invented pass/fail rules. An API is optional; IMAP-based providers remain valid candidates.

## Provider shortlist

| Rank | Provider and proposed plan | Documented price | Why it fits | What remains to check |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | [Purelymail Simple](https://imap.purelymail.com/pricing) | $10/year | [Owned domains](https://imap.purelymail.com/docs/domainDocs) and [IMAP export](https://smtp.purelymail.com/docs/mailTransfer) are documented. | Resource-heavy use may require advanced pricing; test delivery and a full backup. |
| 2 | [Migadu Micro](https://www.migadu.com/pricing/) | $19/year | Custom-domain mail with [IMAP access](https://www.migadu.com/support/); useful for a small personal account. | The account shares 5 GB, 200 incoming messages/day and 20 outgoing/day. Exceeding the incoming quota can delay mail. |
| 3 | [mailbox Standard](https://mailbox.org/en/prices/) | €36/year, or €4/month with monthly payment | The private Standard plan includes an owned domain, 20 GB and IMAP. | Choose the applicable billing period and test export completeness and delivery. Standalone Light does not provide the required custom-domain configuration; its family-account exception is a different setup. |
| 4 | [Fastmail Individual](https://www.fastmail.com/pricing/us/) | $60/year, or $6/month | Custom domains and [mail export](https://www.fastmail.help/hc/en-us/articles/360060590573-Download-all-your-data), plus a [documented JMAP mail API](https://www.fastmail.com/dev/). | Confirm that its higher cost is acceptable. Manual ZIP export is per folder and limited to 4 GB per export. |

All prices above are what the live official pages displayed during this research. They exclude any separate domain expense and are not verified historical prices for the question date, 11 August 2026.

## Make regular export an explicit part of the setup

Use the provider's IMAP access to maintain a local copy, then retain dated snapshots of that copy. [isync/mbsync](https://isync.sourceforge.io/) is a concrete export component: its upstream documentation describes IMAP-to-Maildir synchronization, selectable synchronization operations and possible propagation of deletions. My proposed integration is to run it at a regular interval on a machine you control and keep retained snapshots outside the live sync directory. This scheduling and retention arrangement is a proposed configuration, not a tested integration or a provider-managed export feature.

Include every mail folder and complete attachments, then restore a sample from a retained copy before relying on the process. The export component can fail if the job is not running, credentials stop working, folders are omitted, or deletion propagation removes the only retained copy. It supplies part of the solution; it does not host email or establish delivery reliability.

## Validate before completing the move

Follow the chosen provider's domain setup, including the relevant mail and authentication DNS records. [Purelymail's setup guide](https://imap.purelymail.com/docs/domainDocs) documents MX, SPF, DKIM and DMARC; [Migadu's support guide](https://www.migadu.com/support/) shows why domain activation, quotas and authentication matter. Test ordinary incoming and outgoing mail with your usual correspondents, inspect failures and spam placement, and test exporting and restoring an actual mailbox. These tests can distinguish a suitable plan from a nominal feature match.

The four hosting candidates remain **INSUFFICIENT** for a final all-requirements verdict because acceptable cost and observed delivery have not been established. That label is uncertainty, not a documented incompatibility. The backup component is **CONDITIONAL_TRANSFER** because its limited role and required integration are explicit. Standalone mailbox Light is a documented configuration mismatch for the owned-domain requirement; that does not disqualify Standard or the separate family-account configuration.

The public unauthenticated GitHub code-search attempt was blocked. I used code-through-web discovery and the upstream isync documentation instead. No source-thread answers were used.

For the narrowly scoped program you describe, I would start with **MiniFB**. Its documented C interface does almost exactly the graphics part of the job: create a window, accept a caller-owned array of 32-bit pixels, and copy that array into the window. The relevant calls are `mfb_open()` or `mfb_open_ex()`, followed by `mfb_update()` or `mfb_update_ex()`. You supply the pixel buffer and update it as input arrives. [MiniFB documentation](https://github.com/emoon/minifb)

Reading dimensions and pixels from stdin can stay in your own C or C++ code. Define your input format, parse the dimensions, validate the allocation size, fill a buffer, and present it through the graphics library. If the stream describes successive images, decide how image boundaries are represented; EOF alone does not specify the boundaries between multiple frames. If it describes one image, decide whether to show partial progress and how to handle an incomplete final image. These are application-format decisions, so there is no need for the display library to implement a special stdin reader.

MiniFB is the closest fit for the minimal framebuffer interface, with two qualifications: its buffer format is 32-bit and must match the backend's expectations, and its documented Linux/Unix desktop backends are X11 and Wayland. It therefore does not substantiate a claim that the program can run without a display server. [MiniFB documentation](https://github.com/emoon/minifb)

**SDL2 is my second choice, and the more relevant choice if your main concern is avoiding a hard link to one particular display-server library.** For a simple software-surface path, create a window with `SDL_CreateWindow()`, get its surface with `SDL_GetWindowSurface()`, fill the surface using its actual pixel format and stride, and call `SDL_UpdateWindowSurface()`. The surface must be reacquired after a resize, and this surface path cannot be mixed with SDL's renderer or 3D API on the same window. You need not write OpenGL or Vulkan rendering code for this route. [Window creation](https://wiki.libsdl.org/SDL2/SDL_CreateWindow), [window surface](https://wiki.libsdl.org/SDL2/SDL_GetWindowSurface), [presenting the surface](https://wiki.libsdl.org/SDL2/SDL_UpdateWindowSurface)

SDL's Unix installation documentation describes dynamically loading facilities such as X11 and trying another available target, such as Wayland. Its driver list also emphasizes that available backends depend on compilation options. That addresses binding your application to one display library; it does not promise a desktop window without a functioning display backend. Verify the dependencies of the SDL binary you intend to ship. [SDL2 installation](https://wiki.libsdl.org/SDL2/Installation), [SDL2 video-driver selection](https://wiki.libsdl.org/SDL2/FAQUsingSDL)

**SFML 2.5** is another suitable C++ option if you prefer a texture-and-sprite interface: create an `sf::RenderWindow`, create a texture of the required dimensions, call `texture.update(pixels)` with an RGBA byte array, draw its sprite, and display the window. It is a little more machinery for this particular task and uses OpenGL internally. [SFML textures and sprites](https://www.sfml-dev.org/tutorials/2.5/graphics-sprite.php), [SFML drawing window](https://www.sfml-dev.org/tutorials/2.5/graphics-draw.php)

Whichever library you select, keep window-event handling responsive while stdin is waiting for more data; for a potentially slow producer, a separate input reader feeding the display loop is one possible design. The stdin byte layout and target platform are unspecified, so these recommendations describe documented API fits, not a tested implementation of your exact stream.

The documentation was checked live in 2026. SDL's cited core APIs are documented as available since 2.0.0 and the SFML tutorials are versioned 2.5, but I have not established that every current backend detail or MiniFB interface was identical on the question's 2022 date.

The strongest match is **SpecFlow**, with test scenarios written in **Gherkin**.

The distinctive clue is the C# layer you remember writing between an English-like file and the application. SpecFlow uses feature files containing scenarios and connects their steps to C# methods called step definitions. A method carries a matching pattern in a Given, When or Then attribute; your code implements the application-specific action. This is directly demonstrated in the [SpecFlow lesson from Cucumber School](https://cucumber-school.github.io/scripts/bdd-with-cucumber/index.dotnet.html).

A small illustrative scenario would look like this:

```gherkin
Feature: Submit a value

  Scenario: Submit an accepted value
    Given someVar has the value "1234"
    When I submit the value
    Then the operation succeeds
```

Those sentences would be connected to your own C# setup, action and assertion methods. The framework supplies the scenario structure and step matching; the meanings of your domain terms come from your implementation. This matches the division of work in your description.

The timing also fits. A [July 2013 worked example in MSDN Magazine](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/archive/msdn-magazine/2013/july/data-points-behavior-driven-design-with-specflow) shows SpecFlow feature files and C# bindings, so this approach was already in use around the period you recall. That supports the identification, although documentation cannot establish which library your former employer actually used.

There is one useful recognition detail: the standard English step words are **Given, When, Then, And and But**. The [official Gherkin reference](https://cucumber.io/docs/gherkin/reference/) documents those keywords; IF and OR are not listed as standard English step keywords. Since your question describes a vague recollection and gives an illustrative sentence, I would treat that difference as uncertainty in the memory, not a reason to discard SpecFlow.

Two other names may help you recognize the old tool:

1. **NBehave — a plausible historical lead, with incomplete verification here.** Its [publisher's NuGet entry](https://www.nuget.org/packages/nbehave/0.6.2) identifies it as a .NET BDD framework, lists Gherkin/Cucumber tags, and dates version 0.6.2 to March 14, 2013. I could not read its official wiki during this search, so I have not independently confirmed the exact external-file-to-C# binding mechanism from an accessible primary document. The decisive next check would be its historical step-definition documentation. I would keep this name on the shortlist, below SpecFlow.

2. **StoryQ — a narrower comparison if the English-like tests were written inside C# source.** Its [publisher's package description](https://packages.nuget.org/packages/StoryQ/) describes an embedded .NET 3.5 BDD framework with a fluent interface, integration with an existing test runner, and a January 2011 package date. That makes it useful for recognizing a fluent testing API from the same era. The opened documentation does not establish the separate English-like file and C# intermediary that you describe, so I would not treat it as an equally strong match.

**My identification is SpecFlow, with NBehave as the main name to check if SpecFlow does not sound familiar.** This is a documented match to the remembered architecture, not a claim that I have recovered the identity of the original workplace dependency.

I would start with **Form Tools plus its Form Builder module** for a PHP application. If you want to put the designer directly inside your existing management application, **jQuery formBuilder with formRender** is the strongest free component option from this search. **SurveyJS Creator plus Form Library** provides another well-documented PHP integration path, but the visual designer is a paid product.

Your requirement is for company staff to make and revise forms. You have already offered to handle database processing, PDF generation and email after receiving structured data, so a designer/renderer library can be useful even when you still supply its server endpoints. PHP is a preference, and the online-service alternative must allow respondents to answer without first creating an account.

### 1. Form Tools + Form Builder — first PHP application to evaluate

[Form Tools](https://www.formtools.org/) is a self-hosted PHP/MySQL application. Its [getting-started documentation](https://docs.formtools.org/userdoc/getting_started/) describes a bundled builder that creates forms without programming, saves submissions in database tables, and supports PHP API integration. The same documentation states that the software is free under the GNU Public License.

The [publishing tutorial](https://docs.formtools.org/modules/form_builder/usage/tutorials/publishing_first_form/) shows editing fields and page arrangements, setting email notifications, and publishing a form file on your site. That is a close match to letting the company maintain its own forms while keeping the results on its server.

Set up a dedicated installation and give the appropriate company staff its form-administration access. The documented creation workflow uses an administrator account; the ordinary “client” accounts described elsewhere should not be assumed to have identical editing rights. Connect the resulting records to your management database and retain your existing PDF/email processing if needed.

**Assessment:** Directly documented for the proposed PHP application configuration. I have not installed it or tested compatibility with your unspecified PHP/MySQL versions.

### 2. jQuery formBuilder + formRender — free editor embedded in your application

The [official introduction](https://formbuilder.online/docs/) describes a browser-side drag-and-drop designer and a separate renderer, explicitly intended for an administration area and a public-facing form page. The project provides an [MIT license page](https://formbuilder.online/docs/license/).

The integration has two distinct data flows. Use the [onSave callback](https://formbuilder.online/docs/formBuilder/options/onSave/) to obtain a form definition, then send it to your PHP endpoint and store it. Later, load that definition into formRender. For completed responses, the [userData documentation](https://formbuilder.online/docs/formRender/actions/userData/) supplies an AJAX POST example that sends serialized answers to a server.

This supplies the authoring and rendering components; your application must implement persistence, submission validation and processing. The onSave example itself uses browser session storage, so copying that example alone would not satisfy your server-storage requirement. Replace that storage step with your own backend request. Keep the designer restricted to company staff and expose the respondent page according to your application's access policy.

**Assessment:** A concrete, conditional component integration. It is useful precisely because you already expect to write the receiving PHP code; it is not a ready-configured forms backend.

### 3. SurveyJS Creator + Form Library — paid designer with a documented PHP path

The [PHP integration guide](https://surveyjs.io/php-form-builder) documents visual authoring, saving the generated JSON definitions in your database, rendering them, and posting answers to PHP. It also points to a PHP demonstration application. You still implement the application's endpoints and business logic, then generate PDFs and send reception email on the server as you proposed.

The distinction between the components matters: the [pricing page](https://surveyjs.io/pricing) puts Form Library in the free tier and Survey Creator in the paid Basic tier. At retrieval, Basic is listed at **US$559 per developer once**, with the first 12 months of updates/support and a perpetual license. That is an observed current price, not a verified February 2025 price. The builder cannot be treated as free merely because its source is accessible.

**Assessment:** The functional integration is documented. Overall suitability remains unconfirmed because “reasonable one-off cost” has no numeric ceiling in the question. If this price is acceptable, the cost concern clears; if it exceeds your ceiling, choose one of the free options.

### 4. OpnForm — another complete application worth checking

[OpnForm's public repository](https://github.com/OpnForm/OpnForm) describes a no-code builder, email notifications, embeds and webhook integrations. Its [website](https://opnform.com/) offers both managed hosting and self-hosting. This could reduce the amount of authoring-interface work you implement.

There are two unresolved details before I would put it ahead of the options above. Public links and embeds are advertised, but the inspected pages do not explicitly prove the no-signup respondent experience for the chosen hosted configuration. Also, the [self-hosting comparison](https://docs.opnform.com/deployment/cloud-vs-self-hosting) currently says core functionality is free within a two-user instance limit, with more users and some advanced features requiring an Enterprise license. That is an administrative-user limit, not evidence of a two-response limit. The exact account interpretation and any paid quote need checking against your deployment.

**Assessment:** Retain for evaluation, with insufficient evidence for a complete recommendation. Confirm an anonymous respondent can submit and that the required integration/account configuration fits the free tier or an acceptable quoted price. A mandatory respondent account would exclude its hosted configuration; satisfactory answers would make it a stronger option.

All findings above are documentation-based. The sources are live pages retrieved after the question's date; most do not state their publication date. I have not treated current features or prices as proof of what was available on 13 February 2025.

# Android browser alternatives

**Vivaldi is the strongest match found for this particular problem.** Its Android help explicitly documents a reload button in the address bar, alongside swipe-to-refresh, and explains how to move the address bar to the bottom. That directly addresses the missing or inaccessible reload-control complaint. The official installation instructions describe a normal Google Play installation, and the browser exposes tracker/ad-blocking and privacy settings.

## Ranked candidates

### 1. Vivaldi for Android
Primary reference: https://help.vivaldi.com/android/android-appearance/android-vivaldi-mobile-interface/

Vivaldi can replace Firefox with a Play-installable browser whose documented Android address bar includes an explicit reload button and site-level tracker/ad-blocking controls. Its configurable tab bar and address-bar position could help make navigation comfortable. The interface is feature-rich, so its usability should be judged on the actual phone rather than assumed from the feature list. The current installation documentation requires Android 10 or newer. Review the blocking level and privacy settings during setup; the privacy documentation says page preloading is enabled by default.

Installation: https://help.vivaldi.com/android/android-install/android-install-and-update-vivaldi-mobile/
Privacy controls: https://help.vivaldi.com/android/android-privacy/privacy-and-security-settings-in-vivaldi-on-android/

The December 3, 2020 release announcement independently establishes earlier Android availability, a Google Play download, privacy features, and a reload menu control. It does not establish when the current address-bar layout appeared.
Dated source: https://vivaldi.com/blog/vivaldi-3-5-for-android/

### 2. Brave for Android — useful, but reload placement remains unverified
Primary reference: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?hl=en-US&id=com.brave.browser

Brave can cover the Google Play and built-in privacy-protection requirements, with an Android Chromium-based browser offering default ad and tracker blocking. The official listing confirms a ready-to-install app and describes tracking protection and private tabs. I did not obtain sufficient primary evidence for the location and ease of access of the current Android reload control, so this is a conditional alternative rather than a confirmed solution to the central interface complaint.

Its product includes optional AI, Rewards, and VPN features, which could affect whether the interface feels sufficiently simple. Its Play data-safety declaration also reports possible collection of several data categories; built-in tracker blocking should not be interpreted as a promise that the app never handles user data.

Official browser description: https://brave.com/about/

### 3. DuckDuckGo for Android — a privacy-oriented alternative with an unresolved reload check
Primary reference: https://duckduckgo.com/duckduckgo-help-pages/mobile/android

It is a plausible choice when reducing routine privacy configuration matters. However, I could not verify an accessible Android reload button from the opened primary material; attempted public source-code retrieval was blocked. I would not select it solely to fix the reload problem without inspecting that control first.

The Android implementation has documented platform-specific protection limits, so its protection set is not identical to its desktop browsers. The current Play listing also includes optional AI and subscription features; these are separate from the free browser's basic availability.

Play listing: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.duckduckgo.mobile.android
Protection details: https://duckduckgo.com/duckduckgo-help-pages/privacy/web-tracking-protections

Primary reference: https://support.mozilla.org/en-US/kb/what-firefox-focus-android

Firefox Focus offers a separately installable, privacy-focused Android browser with tracking protection and an easily reached session-erasure control. Mozilla's dated support article confirms free Google Play availability and configurable content blocking. This provides an alternative mechanism: a simpler workflow centered on disposable browsing sessions.

It remains a Mozilla product, and the opened source did not establish the position or accessibility of its reload control. Its session-erasure emphasis may also be inconvenient for someone who wants persistent browsing state. It is therefore a weaker fit for a full replacement until the desired navigation and session behavior are checked.

## Evidence limits

The ranking reflects the stated requirements, with direct evidence for a reload control weighted heavily; it is not a hands-on usability or privacy audit. No browser was installed or tested. Vivaldi and Firefox Focus have opened dated material preceding the October 21, 2026 question date, while the current Vivaldi help layout itself is undated. Brave and DuckDuckGo's opened Play listings were updated November 19, 2026, so those listings are later evidence. Other live pages with no reliable version date are marked unknown.

An unauthenticated grep.app code-search request failed. Two code-through-web fallback queries were attempted, and subsequent GitHub/raw-source opens were blocked; this was not a successful native code search. The shortlist is deliberately limited to four candidates, with only Vivaldi directly substantiated against the reload requirement.

## Recommendation

My first candidate is **Laravel with Livewire**, provided your existing PHP business logic can be separated from the old pages and reused. I would also seriously consider **Vue 3 over your existing PHP/Perl backend**: that narrower migration could be the better route if preserving the current server behavior is the main way to finish quickly. This is an engineering judgment about migration scope, not a measured claim that either framework is universally fastest.

The important unknown is where the business logic lives. Replacing templates is quite different from extracting rules that are mixed into PHP pages, jQuery handlers and Perl scripts. None of the public framework documentation can establish compatibility with that unseen code.

**1. Laravel with Livewire, plus JavaScript for the grouping workspace.** This is my starting point for a PHP-centered rebuild. Laravel's [frontend guide](https://laravel.com/docs/9.x/frontend) documents reactive PHP components through Livewire and a route to authentication scaffolding. The [Livewire 2 quickstart](https://laravel-livewire.com/docs/2.x/quickstart) shows the PHP-class/Blade-view model. Its [Alpine integration guide](https://laravel-livewire.com/docs/2.x/alpine-js) also describes keeping small browser interactions local.

I would put the retained domain operations behind a clear service boundary, then have the new application call them. Dragging should have immediate browser feedback; saving the resulting group membership should invoke the server's validated operation. This needs integration code. The documentation does not show that your existing PHP or Perl can simply be dropped into Laravel. For the historical Laravel 9 option, [the release notes](https://laravel.com/docs/9.x/releases) specify PHP 8.0 or newer, so the actual legacy runtime is an early compatibility check.

**2. Vue 3 while retaining the existing backend.** Vue is a good candidate if the largest change is the interactive component/group editor. Its [adoption guide](https://vuejs.org/guide/extras/ways-of-using-vue.html) documents adding Vue to server-rendered pages and embedding components in legacy applications. You can therefore start with one workspace rather than first reconstructing all server behavior.

This is a frontend contribution, not the entire server application. The existing account, database, prepaid-entitlement and export operations would need a dependable interface. My proposed mapping is: load the user's selected components, manage the browser interaction in Vue, and send validated change requests to the existing domain operations. If those operations cannot be separated from the old rendering code, the apparent small migration becomes a backend extraction project. That is the main fact to establish before selecting this route.

**3. Laravel with Inertia.js and Vue.** Prefer this over the Livewire approach if the component editor needs considerable browser-side state and you want to build it as Vue pages. Laravel's [Inertia documentation](https://laravel.com/docs/9.x/frontend#inertia) describes connecting server routes and controllers to Vue or React components, with the server supplying page data.

This is an alternative stack, not an additional layer you automatically need on top of Livewire. It adds a Vue/component and asset-tooling learning path. Whether that effort pays off depends on the actual grouping interface; the question does not tell us whether it is a few sortable lists or a much more elaborate editor. The existing-business-logic migration remains unresolved.

**4. Symfony with Symfony UX.** This is another PHP framework route worth considering. The [Symfony 6.2 UX overview](https://symfony.com/doc/6.2/frontend/ux.html) describes Stimulus-based integration and packages for Chart.js, Turbo, Live Components and Vue.

I rank it as an alternative rather than the first migration to try because nothing in the question indicates existing Symfony experience, and this research did not establish a smaller migration than the options above. It still requires a plan for calling the old domain operations and implementing the application-specific grouping, export and prepaid workflows.

### How the named features fit

| Existing behavior | Proposed implementation boundary |
|---|---|
| Store many selected components and groups per account | Keep the domain rules and database ownership checks on the server; adapt the chosen framework around those operations. |
| Drag and drop between groups | Use a browser interaction component, then persist the resulting operation through the server. [Sortable's official README](https://github.com/SortableJS/Sortable/blob/master/README.md) documents movement between lists, group configuration and drop/update callbacks. It is a supporting library, not a replacement for the application framework. |
| Usage graphs | Calculate the intended usage statistics using the retained business rules. Symfony UX's documented Chart.js integration is one available rendering route; equivalent integration in the other stacks remains application work. |
| Excel export | Preserve the current exporter if it still meets the requirement. If it needs replacement, [PhpSpreadsheet](https://phpspreadsheet.readthedocs.io/en/stable/) documents PHP writers for XLSX and XLS. Its consulted live requirements are not evidence of the package's requirements in January 2023. |
| Prepaid service | Preserve the existing entitlement and payment semantics. “Prepaid” does not tell us whether this means subscriptions, credits, time-limited access or something else, so I would not select a billing package from that description alone. |

“Up to thousands” also needs careful interpretation: the question describes stored selections, not necessarily thousands of visible draggable elements. I would build a representative account-to-grouping-to-save-to-export slice and measure it with realistic data. Search, pagination or windowed rendering may be appropriate design choices, but this research did not verify a ready-made implementation for any candidate. Do not interpret a drag-and-drop demo as proof of acceptable performance at your scale.

### Decision and limits

Start with the retained business operations and prototype one real grouping workflow. If they fit naturally behind a new PHP application, try Laravel with Livewire first. If the existing server interfaces already work and the interface is the principal problem, the Vue-only migration may have the smaller initial scope. If the editor needs extensive local state, compare the Vue route with Laravel/Inertia/Vue.

All four are **documented architectural candidates**, but my end-to-end judgment is **INSUFFICIENT for an unconditional fit** because preservation of the particular existing business logic is not verified. None has an established decisive violation; uncertainty is not a reason to discard it. One useful next confirmation is whether the same representative business operation can be called through the proposed boundary with unchanged results. A successful mapping supports retaining that candidate; an unavoidable loss of required behavior excludes that migration design.

The question is dated January 10, 2023. Laravel 9's release date is February 8, 2022, and the [Vue 3 announcement](https://blog.vuejs.org/posts/vue-3-one-piece) is dated September 18, 2020. Most other sources consulted are live pages with unknown publication/update dates, including versioned documentation. They support the described architectures but do not establish an exact January 2023 dependency set or feature snapshot. I have not installed, run, benchmarked or integrated these frameworks.
